examTakeaway: Bite cells and Heinz bodies after a new oxidant drug are G6PD deficiency, an X-linked inability to refill glutathione.
scenario: A 20-year-old man develops dark urine two days after primaquine. Hemoglobin is 9 g/dL. The smear shows bite cells and blister cells. A special stain shows Heinz bodies. He is of Mediterranean ancestry. Coombs test is negative, so this is not warm antibody hemolysis.
question: Which enzyme is low?
explanation: Bite cells and Heinz bodies after a new oxidant drug are G6PD deficiency, an X-linked inability to refill glutathione. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase supplies NADPH, and without it hemoglobin denatures into Heinz bodies that the spleen bites out. Pyruvate kinase deficiency is a chronic non-spherocytic hemolysis without oxidant bites. Spectrin loss is hereditary spherocytosis, with round cells and a positive osmotic fragility, not Heinz bodies. A heme-synthesis enzyme defect causes sideroblastic anemia, a production problem. Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency is von Gierke disease, a glycogen storage illness.

examTakeaway: Dark urine on waking, with hemolysis and thrombosis, is loss of the GPI anchor that holds CD55 and CD59.
scenario: A 32-year-old man has cola-colored urine on the first morning void that clears later. Hemoglobin is 10 g/dL and the LDH is high. He has had a mesenteric vein clot. Ham test and flow cytometry show red cells missing CD55 and CD59. Coombs test is negative.
question: Which anchor is missing?
options: GPI anchor for CD55 and CD59
correctAnswer: GPI anchor for CD55 and CD59
explanation: Dark urine on waking, with hemolysis and thrombosis, is loss of the GPI anchor that holds CD55 and CD59. GPI anchor for CD55 and CD59 is the PIGA defect of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, so complement punches the red cell and platelets form clot. Spectrin loss is spherocytosis, without morning hemoglobinuria or unusual clots. A hemoglobin beta chain defect is a thalassemia or sickle syndrome, Coombs negative but not CD55-negative. von Willebrand factor deficiency prolongs bleeding time. ADAMTS13 deficiency is TTP, with schistocytes and low platelets as the lead finding.

examTakeaway: Target cells, a very low MCV, and a raised HbA2 are beta-thalassemia trait, not iron deficiency.
scenario: A 24-year-old man has a hemoglobin of 11 g/dL and an MCV of 68 fL. Ferritin is normal. The smear shows target cells. Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows HbA2 of 6 percent. He has no ring sideroblasts and the iron stain of the marrow is not increased.
question: Which globin is underproduced?
options: Alpha globin of four genes deleted
explanation: Target cells, a very low MCV, and a raised HbA2 are beta-thalassemia trait, not iron deficiency. Beta globin is underproduced, so excess alpha chains and a compensatory rise in delta chains raise HbA2, while ferritin stays normal. Alpha globin of four genes deleted is hydrops fetalis, not a walking adult with HbA2 elevation. A heme enzyme defect makes ring sideroblasts and a high iron. Spectrin loss makes spherocytes, not targets with a high HbA2. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is episodic oxidant hemolysis.

examTakeaway: A very high white count with a low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase and a Philadelphia chromosome is CML, not a leukemoid reaction.
scenario: A 55-year-old man has a white count of 120,000/mm3 with a left shift, including myelocytes, and few blasts. Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase is low. Cytogenetics show a 9;22 translocation. He has no fever and no abscess. The spleen is large.
question: Which fusion drives the count?
explanation: A very high white count with a low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase and a Philadelphia chromosome is CML, not a leukemoid reaction. BCR-ABL is the 9;22 product that drives the granulocyte series, and the enzyme score is low. A leukemoid reaction to infection raises the alkaline phosphatase and has a fever or an abscess, which he lacks. PML-RARA is acute promyelocytic leukemia, with abnormal promyelocytes and bleeding. c-MYC of Burkitt lymphoma is a starry-sky B-cell tumor, not this white count. BCL2 of follicular lymphoma is t(14;18), a slow node disease.

examTakeaway: A child with blasts that mark as TdT-positive and no Auer rods has lymphoblastic leukemia, not myeloid leukemia.
scenario: A 6-year-old boy has bone pain, pallor, and a white count of 40,000/mm3. Blasts fill the marrow. They stain for TdT and do not contain Auer rods. Myeloperoxidase is negative. He has no mediastinal mass.
question: Which lineage are the blasts?
explanation: A child with blasts that mark as TdT-positive and no Auer rods has lymphoblastic leukemia, not myeloid leukemia. Lymphoid blasts are TdT positive and myeloperoxidase negative. Myeloid blasts are often myeloperoxidase positive and may show Auer rods, which are absent. Promyelocytic blasts are a myeloid subset with granules and bleeding. Megakaryocytic blasts are rare and mark for platelets. Erythroid blasts are a rare myeloid variant and are not TdT positive.

examTakeaway: A jaw mass in a child with a starry-sky smear and t(8;14) is c-MYC driving Burkitt lymphoma.
scenario: An 8-year-old boy in equatorial Africa has a rapidly growing mass of the jaw. Biopsy shows medium lymphocytes and pale macrophages scattered through them. Cytogenetics show a translocation of 8 and 14. There is no Philadelphia chromosome and the cells are not TdT-positive blasts filling the marrow.
question: Which gene is moved next to the immunoglobulin promoter?
explanation: A jaw mass in a child with a starry-sky smear and t(8;14) is c-MYC driving Burkitt lymphoma. c-MYC is placed next to the immunoglobulin heavy-chain promoter. BCR-ABL is the 9;22 fusion of chronic myeloid leukemia. BCL2 is t(14;18) of follicular lymphoma, a slow adult node disease. Cyclin D1 is t(11;14) of mantle cell lymphoma. PML-RARA is t(15;17) of acute promyelocytic leukemia.

examTakeaway: Punched-out bones, rouleaux, and light chains in the urine are a plasma-cell clone making immunoglobulin.
scenario: A 68-year-old man has back pain and a creatinine of 2.2 mg/dL. The film shows round holes in the skull. The smear shows stacked red cells. Urine is positive for light chains and negative for a large amount of albumin. Calcium is 11.4 mg/dL. A node biopsy is not the study that was done.
question: Which cell is the clone?
options: A mature small lymphocyte of CLL
explanation: Punched-out bones, rouleaux, and light chains in the urine are a plasma-cell clone making immunoglobulin. Plasma cell clones punch bone, spill light chains that injure the kidney, and coat red cells so they stack. Reed-Sternberg cell is Hodgkin lymphoma, a node disease. Myeloblast with Auer rods is acute myeloid leukemia. Lymphoblast is childhood ALL. A mature small lymphocyte of CLL raises the lymphocyte count and makes smudge cells, not punched-out skull holes.

examTakeaway: The most common inherited clot risk that resists activated protein C is factor V Leiden.
scenario: A 28-year-old woman has a second deep-vein thrombosis. She is not pregnant and has no cancer. The clot formed while she was on a short plane ride. Activated protein C does not prolong her clotting time the way it should. Prothrombin gene testing is negative. Antiphospholipid antibody is negative.
question: Which factor is resistant?
explanation: The most common inherited clot risk that resists activated protein C is factor V Leiden. Factor V with the Leiden change is not cut by activated protein C, so the clotting time fails to lengthen. Factor VIII excess can promote clot but is not the activated-protein-C resistance test. Antithrombin deficiency is a different assay and is rarer. Protein C itself being low is a different disease and would not be described as resistance of the substrate. von Willebrand factor deficiency causes bleeding, not thrombosis.

examTakeaway: Skin necrosis a few days after warfarin in a protein-C deficient patient is a transient hypercoagulable state.
scenario: A 40-year-old woman starts warfarin for a new clot and is not bridged with heparin. On day 3 she has painful black patches of skin on the breasts. Protein C was low on a test drawn before any anticoagulant. Platelets have not fallen. She is not on heparin.
question: Which protein fell first?
explanation: Skin necrosis a few days after warfarin in a protein-C deficient patient is a transient hypercoagulable state. Protein C has a short half-life, so warfarin drops it before the procoagulant factors, and an already low level lets clot form in skin. Platelets from heparin antibodies is HIT, and she is not on heparin and the platelet count has not fallen. ADAMTS13 deficiency is TTP. Factor VIII deficiency bleeds into joints. Fibrinogen in DIC falls with oozing from punctures and a low platelet count, not isolated skin necrosis on day 3 of warfarin.

examTakeaway: Clot and miscarriage with a PTT that does not correct on mixing is an antiphospholipid antibody.
scenario: A 29-year-old woman has had three miscarriages after 10 weeks and a prior leg clot. The PTT is prolonged and does not correct when her plasma is mixed with normal plasma. The confirmatory clotting test shortens when extra phospholipid is added. She has no joint bleeding and factor VIII activity is not low.
question: Which inhibitor is present?
explanation: Clot and miscarriage with a PTT that does not correct on mixing is an antiphospholipid antibody. Antiphospholipid antibody prolongs the PTT in the tube but causes thrombosis in the body, and extra phospholipid corrects the assay. A factor VIII antibody also fails to correct on mixing but causes bleeding, and her factor VIII is not low. Heparin in the sample prolongs the PTT but does not explain recurrent miscarriage. Vitamin K deficiency prolongs the PT more than this story and corrects with mixing if it is a factor deficiency. Hemophilia A is an X-linked factor deficiency that corrects on mixing and bleeds into joints.

examTakeaway: Spherocytes, a high MCHC, and a positive osmotic fragility test that improve after splenectomy are spectrin loss.
scenario: A 15-year-old boy has jaundice and a hemoglobin of 10 g/dL. The smear shows spherocytes and the MCHC is high. Osmotic fragility is increased. Coombs test is negative. His father had the same anemia and improved after the spleen was removed. There are no bite cells.
question: Which membrane protein is weak?
explanation: Spherocytes, a high MCHC, and a positive osmotic fragility test that improve after splenectomy are spectrin loss. Spectrin anchors the membrane, and without it red cells become spheres that the spleen traps. GPI-anchored CD55 loss is nocturnal hemoglobinuria with thrombosis. A beta globin chain defect makes target cells and a high HbA2. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency makes bite cells after an oxidant, which are absent. Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes chronic hemolysis without this spherocyte and high-MCHC pattern.
